chapters.title: הַצָּלַת אִישׁ הַפַּח
chapters.orig_title: The Rescue of the Tin Woodman

w: כְּבָר מִזְּמַן|long since|~lit. already from a while
s.line: When Dorothy awoke the sun was shining through the trees and Toto had long been out chasing birds around him and squirrels.
s.note: רָדַף אַחֲרֵי = chased, literally "pursued after". The verb takes אַחֲרֵי, never a direct object. Hebrew has no "-ing" past: זָרְחָה is simply "shone", and context gives "was shining". כְּבָר מִזְּמַן = "long ago already", very common in speech: הוּא הָלַךְ כְּבָר מִזְּמַן (he left ages ago).

s.line: She sat up and looked around her.
s.note: הִתְיַשֵּׁב (hitpa'el) = to sit down or sit up, the change of position. יָשַׁב (pa'al) = to be sitting. סְבִיבָהּ is סָבִיב (around) with the ending for "her".

s.line: There was the Scarecrow, still standing patiently in his corner, waiting for her.
“We must go and search for water,” she said to him.
s.note: לְחַפֵּשׂ takes a direct object: לְחַפֵּשׂ מַיִם = to look for water, with no word for "for". Two infinitives can follow each other, as in English "go to look": לָלֶכֶת לְחַפֵּשׂ. צְרִיכִים is masculine plural because the "we" includes the Scarecrow.

s.line: “Why do you want water?” he asked.

w: לִי בַּגָּרוֹן|in my throat|~lit. to me in the throat
s.line: “To wash my face clean after the dust of the road, and to drink, so the dry bread will not stick in my throat.”
s.note: נִתְקַע (nif'al; future יִתָּקַע) = to get stuck, an everyday word: נִתְקַעְתִּי בַּפְּקָקִים (I got stuck in traffic). With body parts Hebrew often uses לִי instead of "my": לִי בַּגָּרוֹן = in my throat. הַפָּנִים is plural in form: פָּנִים = face.

s.line: “It must be inconvenient to be made of flesh,” said the Scarecrow thoughtfully, “for you must sleep, and eat and drink.
s.note: מְהֻרְהָר = pensive, lost in thought. Like מְאֻשָּׁר, it is a pu'al participle used as an adjective, from הִרְהֵר (to ponder), a four-letter root. בֶּטַח = "surely, probably", very common in speech; בֶּטַח! alone = "sure!".

w: יֵשׁ לָךְ|you have|~lit. there is to you
s.line: However, you have brains, and it is worth a lot of bother to be able to think properly.”
s.note: עִם זֹאת = "however, even so", a bit formal; you will meet it often in the news. שָׁוֶה = worth: זֶה לֹא שָׁוֶה אֶת זֶה (it isn't worth it). English "brains" is one מֹחַ in Hebrew.

s.line: They left the cottage and walked through the trees until they found a little spring of clear water,

w: אֲרוּחַת הַבֹּקֶר|the breakfast|~lit. meal of the morning
s.line: where Dorothy drank and bathed and ate her breakfast.
s.note: הִתְרַחֵץ (hitpa'el) = to wash oneself, to bathe; רָחַץ (pa'al) = to wash something. The hitpa'el often does the action to yourself: הִתְלַבֵּשׁ = got dressed.

s.line: She saw there was not much bread left in the basket,
s.note: נִשְׁאַר = to remain, be left over (nif'al, but active in meaning). Everyday: לֹא נִשְׁאַר לִי כֶּסֶף (I have no money left).

s.line: and the girl was thankful the Scarecrow did not have to eat anything,
for there was scarcely enough for herself and Toto for the day.
s.note: בְּקֹשִׁי = barely, hardly (from קָשֶׁה, hard): בְּקֹשִׁי יָשַׁנְתִּי (I hardly slept).

w: הַדֶּרֶךְ הָעֲשׂוּיָה לְבֵנִים צְהֻבּוֹת|the yellow brick road|~lit. the road made of yellow bricks
s.line: When she had finished her meal, and was about to go back to the road of yellow brick, she was startled to hear a deep groan near by.
s.note: עָמַד לְ… + infinitive = "was about to": אֲנִי עוֹמֵד לָצֵאת (I'm about to leave), הַסֶּרֶט עוֹמֵד לְהַתְחִיל (the film is about to start).

s.line: “What was that?” she asked timidly.

w: אֵין לִי מֻשָּׂג|I have no idea|~idiom: lit. there is not to me a notion
s.line: “I cannot imagine,” replied the Scarecrow; “but we can go and see.”
s.note: אֵין לִי מֻשָּׂג = "I have no idea", one of the most common phrases in spoken Hebrew. מֻשָּׂג = a concept, a notion.

s.line: Just then another groan reached their ears, and the sound seemed to come from behind them.
s.note: נִשְׁמַע (nif'al of שָׁמַע) = "was heard", and also "sounds, seems by its sound": זֶה נִשְׁמָע טוֹב (that sounds good). The greeting מָה נִשְׁמָע? ("what's new?") is the same verb.

s.line: They turned and walked through the forest a few steps,
when Dorothy discovered something shining in a ray of sunshine that fell between the trees.
s.note: קֶרֶן = a ray (of light), but also a horn and, in modern Hebrew, a fund: קֶרֶן פֶּנְסְיָה (a pension fund).

s.line: She ran to the place and then stopped short, with a little cry of surprise.
s.note: נֶעֱצַר (nif'al) = to stop (oneself), from עָצַר = to stop something. In the news נֶעֱצַר also means "was arrested". בְּבַת אַחַת = all at once, suddenly.

s.line: One of the big trees had been partly chopped through,
and standing beside it, with an uplifted axe in his hands, was a man made entirely of tin.
s.note: מוּרָם (raised) is a hof'al participle, the passive of the hif'il הֵרִים (to lift): הֵרִים אֶת הַגַּרְזֶן → הַגַּרְזֶן מוּרָם. לְיָדוֹ, literally "at his hand", is the normal way to say "next to him".

s.line: His head and arms and legs were jointed upon his body, but he stood perfectly motionless, as if he could not stir at all.
s.note: מְחֻבָּר (pu'al ptc) = connected, attached, the passive of חִבֵּר (pi'el, to connect). You'll see it on screens: מְחֻבָּר = online, connected. כְּאִלּוּ = "as if"; young Israelis also use it as filler, like English "like".

s.line: Dorothy looked at him in amazement, and so did the Scarecrow,
s.note: הִבִּיט בְּ… = to look at; the verb takes בְּ, so "at him" is בּוֹ. תַּדְהֵמָה = astonishment, a word you'll hear in the news: הַיְּדִיעָה הִתְקַבְּלָה בְּתַדְהֵמָה (the news was received with shock).

w: רַגְלֵי הַפַּח|the tin legs|~lit. legs of the tin
לוֹ בַּשִּׁנַּיִם|his teeth|~lit. to him in the teeth
s.line: while Toto barked sharply and made a snap at the tin legs, which hurt his teeth.
s.note: הִכְאִיב לְ… (hif'il) = to hurt someone, to cause pain (כְּאֵב). Compare כּוֹאֵב לִי = it hurts me, כּוֹאֵב לִי הָרֹאשׁ = I have a headache.

s.line: “Did you groan?” asked Dorothy.
s.note: A yes/no question in spoken Hebrew is just a statement with a rising voice: <t>אַתָּה נֶאֱנַקְתָּ?</t> = "did you groan?". Formal writing adds <t>הַאִם</t> at the start.

s.line: “Yes,” answered the tin man, “I did.

w: וְאַף אֶחָד|and no one|~with לֹא: nobody
s.line: I’ve been groaning for more than a year, and no one has ever heard me before or come to help me.”
s.note: "I have been doing X for a year" is the present + כְּבָר in Hebrew: אֲנִי נֶאֱנָק כְּבָר שָׁנָה, like אֲנִי גָּר פֹּה כְּבָר שָׁנָה (I've lived here for a year). עָזַר לְ… takes לְ: help to me, לַעֲזֹר לִי.

s.line: “What can I do for you?” she inquired softly, for she was moved by the sad voice in which the man spoke.
s.note: נָגַע לְלִבּוֹ = "touched his heart", moved him. Note the preposition: נָגַע בְּ… = to touch something physically, נָגַע לְ… = to concern or move someone: זֶה לֹא נוֹגֵעַ לְךָ (it's none of your business).

w: פַּחִית שֶׁמֶן|an oil-can|~lit. a can of oil
s.line: “Get an oil-can and oil my joints,” he answered.
s.note: Spoken Hebrew usually gives orders with the future instead of the imperative: תָּבִיאִי ("you will bring") rather than הָבִיאִי. פַּחִית = a can (of drink, of oil), a small cousin of פַּח (tin, sheet metal). שִׁמֵּן (pi'el) = to oil, to grease, from שֶׁמֶן.

s.line: “They are rusted so badly that I cannot move them at all;
s.note: לָזוּז (pa'al) = to move yourself; לְהָזִיז (hif'il) = to move something else. זוּז! = move!, get out of the way; תָּזִיז אֶת הָאוֹטוֹ = move the car.

s.line: if I am well oiled I shall soon be all right again.
s.note: מְשֻׁמָּן (oiled, greasy) is the pu'al participle of שִׁמֵּן: pi'el = active, pu'al = passive. Same pattern as חִבֵּר → מְחֻבָּר in the last part.

s.line: You will find an oil-can on a shelf in my cottage.”
Dorothy at once ran back to the cottage and found the oil-can,
s.note: פַּחִית הַשֶּׁמֶן: in a construct pair the הַ goes on the second word only. פַּחִית שֶׁמֶן = an oil-can, פַּחִית הַשֶּׁמֶן = the oil-can.

s.line: and then she returned and asked anxiously, “Where are your joints?”

w: חוֹטֵב הָעֵצִים מִפַּח|the Tin Woodman|~lit. the woodcutter of tin
s.line: “Oil my neck, first,” replied the Tin Woodman.
s.note: Baum calls him the "Tin Woodman". In full he is חוֹטֵב הָעֵצִים מִפַּח, the woodcutter made of tin. חוֹטֵב is the participle of חָטַב (to chop wood). From here on this edition calls him by his short name, אִישׁ הַפַּח, "the tin man".

s.line: So she oiled it,

w: בְּרֹאשׁ הַפַּח|the tin head|~lit. in the head of the tin
s.line: and as it was quite badly rusted the Scarecrow took hold of the tin head and moved it gently from side to side until it worked freely,
s.note: אָחַז בְּ… = to grip, take hold of, with בְּ. Here both verbs of moving appear side by side: the Scarecrow הֵזִיז (hif'il) the head until it זָז (pa'al) by itself.

s.line: and then the man could turn it himself.
s.note: בְּעַצְמוֹ = by himself, on his own: בְּעַצְמִי (by myself), בְּעַצְמָהּ (by herself). לְסוֹבֵב = to turn something; הִסְתּוֹבֵב, earlier in this chapter, = to turn oneself around.

s.line: “Now oil the joints in my arms,” he said.

w: כְּמוֹ חֲדָשִׁים|as good as new|~lit. like new
s.line: And Dorothy oiled them and the Scarecrow bent them carefully until they were quite free from rust and as good as new.
s.note: כְּמוֹ חָדָשׁ = "as good as new", a phrase you'll see in every second-hand ad: יָד שְׁנִיָּה, כְּמוֹ חָדָשׁ. חֲלֻדָּה (rust) and חָלוּד (rusty) share the root ח־ל־ד.

s.line: The Tin Woodman gave a sigh of satisfaction and lowered his axe, which he leaned against the tree.
s.note: Don't mix up נֶאֱנַח (sighed, root א־נ־ח) and נֶאֱנַק (groaned, root א־נ־ק): both are nif'al and differ only in the last letter. הוֹרִיד is the hif'il (causative) of יָרַד: "made go down" = lowered, took down. Today it also means "to download".

s.line: “This is a great comfort,” he said.
s.note: אֵיזוֹ הֲקָלָה! = "what a relief!", the everyday exclamation. הֲקָלָה comes from קַל (light, easy); in the news it also means an easing of rules: הֲקָלוֹת.

s.line: “I have been holding that axe in the air ever since I rusted, and I’m glad to be able to put it down at last.
s.note: Again the present for "have been …ing": אֲנִי מַחֲזִיק … מֵאָז. הֶחֱלִיד (hif'il) = to rust, to go rusty. סוֹף סוֹף = finally, at last (said with relief).

s.line: Now, if you will oil the joints of my legs, I shall be all right once more.”
So they oiled his legs until he could move them freely;

w: וַאֲסִיר תּוֹדָה|and grateful|~idiom: lit. prisoner of thanks
s.line: and he thanked them again and again for his release, for he seemed a very polite creature, and very grateful.
s.note: אֲסִיר תּוֹדָה = grateful, literally "a prisoner of thanks"; for a woman אֲסִירַת תּוֹדָה. הוֹדָה לְ… עַל … = to thank someone for something, the same root as תּוֹדָה. אוֹתָן in the last sentence is feminine because רַגְלַיִם is feminine.

w: הֱיִיתֶם בָּאִים|you had come|~hypothetical: were coming
הָיִיתִי עוֹמֵד|I would have stood|~hypothetical: was standing
s.line: “I might have stood there always if you had not come along,” he said;
s.note: For "if … had …, … would have …", Hebrew uses הָיָה + participle in both halves: אִם לֹא הֱיִיתֶם בָּאִים, הָיִיתִי עוֹמֵד. Everyday: אִם הָיִיתִי יוֹדֵעַ, הָיִיתִי בָּא (if I had known, I would have come).

s.line: “so you have certainly saved my life.
How did you happen to be here?”
“We are on our way to the Emerald City to see the Great Oz,” she answered, “and we stopped at your cottage to pass the night.”
s.note: בִּלָּה (pi'el) = to spend time, and also to have a good time, go out: בִּלִּינוּ יָפֶה (we had a nice time), בִּלּוּי = an outing, entertainment. בַּדֶּרֶךְ לְ… = on the way to.

s.line: “Why do you wish to see Oz?” he asked.
“I want him to send me back to Kansas, and the Scarecrow wants him to put a few brains into his head,” she replied.
s.note: "I want him to do X" cannot be said with an infinitive in Hebrew. It is רוֹצֶה שֶׁ… + future: אֲנִי רוֹצָה שֶׁהוּא יַחְזִיר אוֹתִי, literally "I want that he will return me". הֶחְזִיר (hif'il of חָזַר) = to bring or give back.

w: שֶׁאִישׁ הַפַּח|as if the Tin Woodman
s.line: The Tin Woodman appeared to think deeply for a moment.
s.note: שָׁקַע בְּמַחְשָׁבוֹת = "sank into thoughts", was lost in thought. שָׁקַע is literally "sank": הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ שׁוֹקַעַת (the sun is setting), הַסְּפִינָה שָׁקְעָה (the ship sank).

s.line: Then he said:
“Do you suppose Oz could give me a heart?”
s.note: יוּכַל is the future of יָכֹל (can), and it is irregular: אוּכַל, תּוּכַל, יוּכַל. In questions like this the future gives "could, would be able to".

w: נִרְאֶה לִי|I guess|~idiom: lit. it seems to me
s.line: “Why, I guess so,” Dorothy answered.
s.note: נִרְאֶה לִי = "it seems to me, I think", very common in speech: נִרְאֶה לִי שֶׁהוּא צוֹדֵק (I think he's right). שֶׁכֵּן = "that yes", so; שֶׁלֹּא = "that not": נִרְאֶה לִי שֶׁלֹּא = I guess not.

s.line: “It would be as easy as to give the Scarecrow brains.”
“True,” the Tin Woodman returned.
s.note: הֵשִׁיב (hif'il of שָׁב, to return) = to reply, a more literary word than עָנָה. You'll see הֵשִׁיב in news reports: הַשַּׂר הֵשִׁיב עַל הַשְּׁאֵלָה.

s.line: “So, if you will allow me to join your party, I will also go to the Emerald City and ask Oz to help me.”
s.note: הִצְטָרֵף (to join) is a hitpa'el of צ־ר־ף. When the root starts with צ, the ת of the hitpa'el swaps places with it and becomes ט: not הִתְצָרֵף but הִצְטָרֵף. בִּקֵּשׁ מִ… = to ask someone (for something), with מִ: בִּקַּשְׁתִּי מִמֶּנּוּ = I asked him.

s.line: “Come along,” said the Scarecrow heartily,
and Dorothy added that she would be pleased to have his company.
s.note: Reported speech keeps the tense of the original words: she said "I will be glad", so Hebrew writes שֶׁהִיא תִּשְׂמַח (future), where English has "would". חֶבְרָה = company, both "companionship" and "a firm": הוּא עוֹבֵד בְּחֶבְרַת הַיְטֵק (he works at a tech company).

s.line: So the Tin Woodman shouldered his axe and they all passed through the forest until they came to the road that was paved with yellow brick.
s.note: סָלוּל (paved) is the pa'ul participle of סָלַל (to pave). Notice דֶּרֶךְ twice here: as a preposition, דֶּרֶךְ הַיַּעַר = through the forest; as a noun, הַדֶּרֶךְ = the road (feminine, hence הַסְּלוּלָה).

s.line: The Tin Woodman had asked Dorothy to put the oil-can in her basket.
“For,” he said, “if I should get caught in the rain, and rust again, I would need the oil-can badly.”
s.note: נִתְפַּס (nif'al of תָּפַס, to catch) = to be caught: נִתְפַּסְנוּ בַּגֶּשֶׁם (we got caught in the rain), and in the news הַגַּנָּב נִתְפַּס (the thief was caught). זָקוּק לְ… = in need of, a little more formal than צָרִיךְ: אֲנִי זָקוּק לְעֶזְרָה.

w: הָיָה לָהֶם מַזָּל|they were lucky|~idiom: lit. there was luck to them
s.line: It was a bit of good luck to have their new comrade join the party,
s.note: הָיָה לִי מַזָּל = I was lucky, literally "there was luck to me", the same pattern as יֵשׁ לִי. מַזָּל טוֹב! = congratulations.

s.line: for soon after they had begun their journey again they came to a place where the trees and branches grew so thick over the road that the travelers could not pass.
s.note: שֶׁבּוֹ = "in which", the usual way to say "where" after a noun: הַמָּקוֹם שֶׁבּוֹ גָּרְתִּי (the place where I lived). מְטַיֵּל = a traveler, hiker, tourist, from טִיֵּל (pi'el, to take a trip, go for a walk).

w: נִגַּשׁ לָעֲבוֹדָה|set to work|~idiom: lit. approached the work
s.line: But the Tin Woodman set to work with his axe and chopped so well that soon he cleared a passage for the entire party.
s.note: פִּנָּה (pi'el) = to clear out, vacate: פִּנּוּ אֶת הַבִּנְיָן (they evacuated the building). It is spelled and pointed exactly like the noun פִּנָּה (corner); only the context tells you which one it is.

s.line: Dorothy was thinking so earnestly as they walked along that she did not notice when the Scarecrow stumbled into a hole and rolled over to the side of the road.
s.note: שָׂם לֵב = to notice, literally "to put heart": לֹא שַׂמְתִּי לֵב (I didn't notice). שִׂים לֵב! = watch out!, pay attention! שָׁקוּעַ בְּ… (pa'ul participle of שָׁקַע) = absorbed in: הוּא שָׁקוּעַ בַּטֶּלֶפוֹן (he's glued to his phone).

s.line: Indeed he was obliged to call to her to help him up again.
s.note: נֶאֱלַץ (nif'al) = was forced, had to. A news word: הַמָּטוֹס נֶאֱלַץ לִנְחֹת (the plane was forced to land). The noun is אִלּוּץ, constraint: אִלּוּצִים = constraints, limitations.

s.line: “Why didn’t you walk around the hole?” asked the Tin Woodman.
s.note: עָקַף = to go around, bypass, and on the road "to overtake": אָסוּר לַעֲקֹף (no overtaking). כְּבִישׁ עֹקֶף = a bypass road.

s.line: “I don’t know enough,” replied the Scarecrow cheerfully.
“My head is stuffed with straw, you know, and that is why I am going to Oz to ask him for some brains.”
s.note: מְמֻלָּא (pu'al ptc) = filled, stuffed, the passive of מִלֵּא (pi'el, to fill). On a menu, פִּלְפֵּל מְמֻלָּא = stuffed pepper. בִּגְלַל זֶה = because of this, that's why.

s.line: “Oh, I see,” said the Tin Woodman.
s.note: "I see" in Hebrew is the past tense הֵבַנְתִּי, "I (have) understood". הֵבַנְתָּ? = got it?

w: בְּסוֹפוֹ שֶׁל דָּבָר|after all|~idiom: lit. at the end of the matter
s.line: “But, after all, brains are not the best things in the world.”
s.note: בְּסוֹפוֹ שֶׁל דָּבָר = "in the end, after all", a fixed phrase in both speech and writing. In speech זֶה often serves as "is" between a subject and its description: מֹחַ זֶה לֹא הַכֹּל (brains aren't everything).

w: וְיֵשׁ לְךָ|and do you have|~lit. and is there to you
s.line: “Have you any?” inquired the Scarecrow.
“No, my head is quite empty,” answered the Woodman.

w: הָיָה לִי|I had|~lit. there was to me
s.line: “But once I had brains, and a heart also;
so, having tried them both, I should much rather have a heart.”
s.note: מַעֲדִיף (hif'il) = to prefer: אֲנִי מַעֲדִיף קָפֶה, מָה אַתָּה מַעֲדִיף?. נִסָּה (pi'el) = to try, try out; נִסָּיוֹן = an attempt, also experience.

s.line: “And why is that?” asked the Scarecrow.
“I will tell you my story, and then you will know.”
s.note: סִפֵּר (pi'el) = to tell, and סִפּוּר = a story, from the same root ס־פ־ר as סֵפֶר (book) and סָפַר (pa'al, to count). תֵּדַע is the future of יָדַע: the י of the root drops out.

s.line: So, while they were walking through the forest, the Tin Woodman told the following story:
s.note: הַבָּא, literally "the coming one", = the next, the following: בַּשָּׁבוּעַ הַבָּא (next week), הַתַּחֲנָה הַבָּאָה (the next stop). בָּרוּךְ הַבָּא = welcome.

w: לְחוֹטֵב עֵצִים|to a woodcutter|pa'al ptc · ח־ט־ב
s.line: “I was born the son of a woodman who chopped down trees in the forest and sold the wood for a living.
s.note: נוֹלַד (nif'al of י־ל־ד) = was born, a true passive. הִתְפַּרְנֵס = to earn a living, from פַּרְנָסָה (livelihood): מִמָּה הוּא מִתְפַּרְנֵס? = what does he do for a living? עֵצִים means both "trees" and "wood".

s.line: When I grew up, I too became a wood-chopper, and after my father died I took care of my old mother as long as she lived.
s.note: נַעֲשָׂה (nif'al of עָשָׂה) = to become; in speech you'll more often hear נִהְיָה: נִהְיָה קַר (it got cold). טִפֵּל בְּ… = to take care of, with בְּ; טִפּוּל = care, treatment. כָּל עוֹד = as long as.

s.line: Then I made up my mind that instead of living alone I would marry, so that I might not become lonely.
s.note: הִתְחַתֵּן עִם … = to marry someone: the verb is reflexive (hitpa'el) and takes עִם, never a direct object. כְּדֵי שֶׁ… = so that, followed by the future: כְּדֵי שֶׁלֹּא אֶהְיֶה בּוֹדֵד.

w: בְּכָל לִבִּי|with all my heart|~set phrase
s.line: “There was one of the Munchkin girls who was so beautiful that I soon grew to love her with all my heart.
s.note: הִתְאַהֵב בְּ… (hitpa'el of א־ה־ב) = to fall in love with: הִתְאַהַבְתִּי בָּהּ. אָהַב = to love, the state; הִתְאַהֵב = to fall in love, the event.

s.line: She, on her part, promised to marry me as soon as I could earn enough money to build a better house for her;
s.note: הִרְוִיחַ (hif'il) = to earn, to profit: הוּא מַרְוִיחַ טוֹב (he earns well); רֶוַח = profit. בְּרֶגַע שֶׁ… = "the moment that", as soon as. מִצִּדָּהּ = from her side, for her part; מִצִּדִּי = as far as I'm concerned.

s.line: so I set to work harder than ever.
But the girl lived with an old woman who did not want her to marry anyone,

w: עֲבוֹדוֹת הַבַּיִת|the housework|~lit. works of the house
s.line: for she was so lazy she wished the girl to remain with her and do the cooking and the housework.

w: לַמְּכַשֵּׁפָה הָרָעָה מֵהַמִּזְרָח|to the Wicked Witch of the East
s.line: So the old woman went to the Wicked Witch of the East, and promised her two sheep and a cow if she would prevent the marriage.
s.note: מָנַע = to prevent; מְנִיעָה = prevention. Its nif'al נִמְנַע = to refrain, and in the news to abstain: שְׁנֵי חֲבֵרִים נִמְנְעוּ בַּהַצְבָּעָה (two members abstained in the vote). שְׁנֵי כְּבָשִׂים: כֶּבֶשׂ is masculine, so "two" is שְׁנֵי, not שְׁתֵּי.

s.line: Thereupon the Wicked Witch enchanted my axe,
s.note: בְּעִקְבוֹת = "in the footsteps of", following, as a result of. A very common news phrase: בְּעִקְבוֹת הַסְּעָרָה (following the storm). כִּשֵּׁף (pi'el) = to bewitch; מְכַשֵּׁפָה is its participle.

w: בְּכָל הַכֹּחַ|with all my strength|~set phrase
כְּמָה שֶׁיּוֹתֵר מַהֵר|as soon as possible|~set phrase: lit. as much as more quickly
s.line: and when I was chopping away at my best one day, for I was anxious to get the new house and my wife as soon as possible, the axe slipped all at once and cut off my left leg.
s.note: כְּמָה שֶׁיּוֹתֵר מַהֵר = as soon as possible, the spoken form; in writing you'll see בְּהֶקְדֵּם הָאֶפְשָׁרִי. הֶחֱלִיק = to slip, and also to skate or slide; קָטַע = to cut off, and also to interrupt: אַל תִּקְטַע אוֹתִי! (don't interrupt me!). רֶגֶל is feminine, hence הַשְּׂמָאלִית.

s.line: “This at first seemed a great misfortune, for I knew a one-legged man could not do very well as a wood-chopper.
s.note: אָסוֹן = a disaster, a news word: אֲסוֹן טֶבַע (natural disaster). In speech it is also a cheerful exaggeration: אֵיזֶה אָסוֹן!. Inside "I knew that…" Hebrew keeps the present יָכוֹל, where English says "could".

s.line: So I went to a tinsmith and had him make me a new leg out of tin.
s.note: פֶּחָח = a tinsmith, from פַּח. In modern Israel the פֶּחָח is the auto-body repairman you take your car to after an accident. הִזְמִין = to order (also to invite); אֵצֶל = at someone's place: הִזְמַנְתִּי אֶצְלוֹ = I ordered from him.

w: אַחֲרֵי שֶׁהִתְרַגַּלְתִּי|after I got used|hitpa'el · ר־ג־ל
s.line: The leg worked very well, once I was used to it.
s.note: הִתְרַגֵּל לְ… (hitpa'el) = to get used to; its root letters ר־ג־ל are the same as in רֶגֶל (leg) and רָגִיל (ordinary, used to). מְצֻיָּן = excellent, another pu'al participle that works as an everyday adjective, like מְאֻשָּׁר.

w: הַמְּכַשֵּׁפָה הָרָעָה מֵהַמִּזְרָח|the Wicked Witch of the East
s.line: But my action angered the Wicked Witch of the East, for she had promised the old woman I should not marry the pretty Munchkin girl.
s.note: כָּעַס (pa'al) = to be angry; הִכְעִיס (hif'il) = to make someone angry: זֶה מַכְעִיס אוֹתִי (that makes me angry). Hif'il is often "cause to": יָרַד → הוֹרִיד, כָּעַס → הִכְעִיס.

s.line: When I began chopping again, my axe slipped and cut off my right leg.
Again I went to the tinsmith, and again he made me a leg out of tin.
After this the enchanted axe cut off my arms, one after the other;
s.note: מְכֻשָּׁף (pu'al ptc) = bewitched, enchanted, the passive of כִּשֵּׁף: the witch כִּשְּׁפָה the axe, so the axe is מְכֻשָּׁף. אַחַת אַחֲרֵי הַשְּׁנִיָּה is feminine because זְרוֹעַ is feminine.

s.line: but, nothing daunted, I had them replaced with tin ones.
s.note: וִתֵּר (pi'el) = to give up: אַל תְּוַתֵּר! (don't give up!). דָּאַג has three common uses: דָּאַג = worried, דָּאַג לְ… = took care of, דָּאַג שֶׁ… = made sure that. הֶחְלִיף X בְּ־Y = to replace X with Y.

s.line: The Wicked Witch then made the axe slip and cut off my head, and at first I thought that was the end of me.
s.note: גָּרַם לְ־X לְ… = "made X do …", caused X to: הִיא גָּרְמָה לַגַּרְזֶן לְהַחְלִיק. Everyday: זֶה גָּרַם לִי לִצְחֹק (that made me laugh).

s.line: But the tinsmith happened to come along, and he made me a new head out of tin.
s.note: בְּמִקְרֶה = by chance. In a question it means "by any chance": אַתָּה בְּמִקְרֶה יוֹדֵעַ אֵיפֹה הַתַּחֲנָה? (do you happen to know where the station is?).

s.line: “I thought I had beaten the Wicked Witch then, and I worked harder than ever;
s.note: נִצֵּחַ (pi'el) = to beat, to win: נִצַּחְנוּ! (we won!), נִצָּחוֹן = victory. Hebrew has no pluperfect: "I had beaten" is the simple past נִצַּחְתִּי.

w: הָיָה לִי מֻשָּׂג|I had no idea|~idiom: lit. there was to me a notion
s.line: but I little knew how cruel my enemy could be.
s.note: אֵין לִי מֻשָּׂג in the past: לֹא הָיָה לִי מֻשָּׂג = I had no idea. אוֹיֶבֶת is the feminine of אוֹיֵב (enemy), because the enemy is the Witch.

s.line: She thought of a new way to kill my love for the beautiful Munchkin maiden, and made my axe slip again, so that it cut right through my body, splitting me into two halves.
s.note: חִלֵּק (pi'el) = to divide, to split, or to hand out: חִלֵּק פְּרָסִים (handed out prizes). Without vowels חלק is also חֵלֶק (a part) and חָלָק (smooth); the same three letters give הֶחֱלִיק (slipped). דֶּרֶךְ (way) is feminine: דֶּרֶךְ חֲדָשָׁה.

w: בָּא לְעֶזְרָתִי|came to my help|~set phrase
s.line: Once more the tinsmith came to my help and made me a body of tin,
fastening my tin arms and legs and head to it, by means of joints, so that I could move around as well as ever.
s.note: בְּעֶזְרַת = "with the help of", by means of: בְּעֶזְרַת הַשֵּׁם (God willing, lit. with God's help), a phrase Israelis say all the time. חִבֵּר (pi'el, to connect) is the active partner of מְחֻבָּר (pu'al, connected) from earlier in the chapter.

w: אוֹי וַאֲבוֹי|alas|~set phrase: lit. oh and woe
s.line: But, alas!

w: הָיָה לִי|I had|~lit. there was to me
הָיָה אִכְפַּת לִי|I cared|~idiom: lit. it was of concern to me
s.line: I had now no heart, so that I lost all my love for the Munchkin girl, and did not care whether I married her or not.
s.note: אִכְפַּת לִי = I care, it matters to me; much more common in the negative: לֹא אִכְפַּת לִי = I don't care. Past: לֹא הָיָה אִכְפַּת לִי. אִבֵּד (pi'el) = to lose something; אָבַד (pa'al) = to be lost.

s.line: I suppose she is still living with the old woman, waiting for me to come after her.
s.note: מַנִּיחַ = I suppose, assume. It is the same verb as לְהַנִּיחַ (to put down, place) earlier in this chapter: to "lay down" an idea is to assume it. הַנָּחָה = an assumption, and also a discount in a shop. חִכָּה שֶׁ… + future = to wait for something to happen.

w: לֹא הָיָה מְשַׁנֶּה|it did not matter|~idiom: lit. it was not changing
s.line: “My body shone so brightly in the sun that I felt very proud of it and it did not matter now if my axe slipped, for it could not cut me.
s.note: לֹא מְשַׁנֶּה, literally "it doesn't change", = "it doesn't matter, never mind", one of the most useful phrases in spoken Hebrew. גֵּאֶה בְּ… = proud of, with בְּ: אֲנִי גֵּאֶה בְּךָ.

s.line: There was only one danger—that my joints would rust;

w: שֶׁהָיָה צָרִיךְ|that it was needed|~impersonal: it was necessary
s.line: but I kept an oil-can in my cottage and took care to oil myself whenever I needed it.
s.note: אֶת עַצְמִי = myself, as the object of a verb: לְשַׁמֵּן אֶת עַצְמִי. The same עֶצֶם gives בְּעַצְמִי (by myself). הֶחְזִיק = to hold and also to keep (something somewhere).

s.line: However, there came a day when I forgot to do this,
and, being caught in a rainstorm, before I thought of the danger my joints had rusted, and I was left to stand in the woods until you came to help me.
It was a terrible thing to undergo,
s.note: עָבַר = to pass, and also to go through, experience: עָבַרְתִּי יוֹם קָשֶׁה (I had a hard day), הוּא עָבַר הַרְבֵּה (he's been through a lot).

w: הָיָה לִי|I had|~lit. there was to me
הַגְּדוֹלָה בְּיוֹתֵר|the greatest|~lit. the big in most
s.line: but during the year I stood there I had time to think that the greatest loss I had known was the loss of my heart.
s.note: הַגָּדוֹל בְּיוֹתֵר = the biggest, the more formal superlative; in speech הֲכִי גָּדוֹל. חָוָה = to experience, a modern-sounding word with a familiar noun: חֲוָיָה = an experience. אֲבֵדָה = a loss; אֲבֵדוֹת in the news = casualties.

s.line: While I was in love I was the happiest man on earth;
s.note: מְאֹהָב (in love) is a pu'al participle, like מְאֻשָּׁר right next to it. The ה can't take a dagesh, so the א gets a holam instead of a kubutz.

w: מִי שֶׁאֵין לוֹ|whoever has no|~lit. who there is not to him
s.line: but no one can love who has not a heart, and so I am resolved to ask Oz to give me one.
s.note: נָחוּשׁ = determined, resolved, a word from news and speeches: הַמֶּמְשָׁלָה נְחוּשָׁה לְ… (the government is determined to …). מִי שֶׁ… = whoever, anyone who: מִי שֶׁרוֹצֶה, יָכוֹל לָבוֹא.

s.line: If he does, I will go back to the Munchkin maiden and marry her.”
Both Dorothy and the Scarecrow had been greatly interested in the story of the Tin Woodman,
s.note: גַּם … וְגַם … = both … and …. הִתְעַנְיֵן בְּ… (hitpa'el) = to be interested in, with בְּ: אֲנִי מִתְעַנְיֵן בְּהִיסְטוֹרְיָה. מְעַנְיֵן! = interesting!

s.line: and now they knew why he was so anxious to get a new heart.
“All the same,” said the Scarecrow, “I shall ask for brains instead of a heart;
s.note: בְּכָל זֹאת = still, nevertheless, all the same, very common in speech: יָרַד גֶּשֶׁם, וּבְכָל זֹאת יָצָאנוּ (it rained, and we went out anyway).

w: הָיָה לוֹ|he had|~lit. there was to him
s.line: for a fool would not know what to do with a heart if he had one.”
“I shall take the heart,” returned the Tin Woodman; “for brains do not make one happy, and happiness is the best thing in the world.”
s.note: אֶקַּח is the future of לָקַח: the ל drops out, as with נ-roots: אֶקַּח, תִּקַּח, יִקַּח. אֹשֶׁר (happiness) and מְאֻשָּׁר (happy) share the root א־שׁ־ר. עָשָׂה אֶת X מְאֻשָּׁר = made X happy.

s.line: Dorothy did not say anything, for she was puzzled to know which of her two friends was right,
s.note: הִתְלַבֵּט (hitpa'el) = to be torn, to go back and forth over a decision: אֲנִי מִתְלַבֵּט אִם לִנְסֹעַ (I can't decide whether to go). לִבְטוּט = a dilemma. צוֹדֵק = right (about something): אַתָּה צוֹדֵק = you're right.

w: לֹא כָּל כָּךְ מְשַׁנֶּה|it does not matter so much|~idiom: lit. it doesn't change so much
s.line: and she decided if she could only get back to Kansas and Aunt Em, it did not matter so much whether the Woodman had no brains and the Scarecrow no heart, or each got what he wanted.
What worried her most was that the bread was nearly gone,
s.note: הִדְאִיג (hif'il) = to worry someone, the causative of דָּאַג (to worry): זֶה מַדְאִיג = that's worrying. נִגְמַר (nif'al) = to end, to run out: נִגְמַר הֶחָלָב (the milk ran out), נִגְמַר לִי הַכֶּסֶף (I ran out of money).

s.line: and another meal for herself and Toto would empty the basket.
To be sure, neither the Woodman nor the Scarecrow ever ate anything,
but she was not made of tin nor straw, and could not live unless she was fed.
s.note: עָשׂוּי מִ… (pa'ul participle of עָשָׂה) = made of: עָשׂוּי מֵעֵץ (made of wood). Here it is feminine, עֲשׂוּיָה, because it describes Dorothy.
